lesson.title: Have-Hunger & Co
lesson.subtitle: Feelings as possessions with avoir: avoir faim, soif, peur, raison, besoin de.

hook.title: Possessing Your Sensations: The Complete avoir Idiom Set
hook.content: Alongside avoir faim ('be hungry'), avoir soif ('be thirsty'), avoir peur ('be afraid'), avoir raison ('be right'), and avoir besoin de ('need'), French also says J'ai froid ('I feel cold') and J'ai chaud ('I feel hot')!

footnotes.title: Why 'Je suis chaud / froid' is a dangerous trap in French!
footnotes.content: If a person wants to say 'I feel cold / hot', they MUST say J'ai froid / J'ai chaud ('I have cold / heat')!

pattern.title: Person Feels State → J'ai faim / soif / froid / chaud / peur / raison
pattern.content: Keep every personal sensation and need in the avoir column, with no article before the state noun.
pattern.linguist_note: Experiencer-possessor idioms with avoir + bare noun form a cohesive semantic class in Gallo-Romance.
pattern.trap_note: Never say *Je suis froid when you are shivering — say J'ai froid ('I have cold')!

exercises.prompt: Match each avoir sensation with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.german: I feel cold / I feel hot

matching_pairs.english: Tu as raison / Tu as tort
matching_pairs.german: You are right / You are wrong

exercises.target_answer: I'm hungry / I'm thirsty, I feel cold / I feel hot, You are right / You are wrong, I'm afraid of that, I need to leave
exercises.meaning: J'ai faim / J'ai soif, J'ai froid / J'ai chaud, Tu as raison / Tu as tort, J'ai peur de ça, J'ai besoin de partir
exercises.explanation: Every one of these states is possessed with avoir in French.

exercises.prompt: You are sitting outside in winter and shivering. How do you say 'I am cold'?
exercises.meaning: I am cold (lit. I have cold)
exercises.explanation: A person feeling cold or hot always uses avoir: J'ai froid / J'ai chaud.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentences match 'J'ai besoin de comprendre'?
renderings: I have a need to understand
exercises.explanation: avoir besoin de + bare infinitive means 'to need to [do something]'.

exercises.idea: are you hungry or are you thirsty
cues: Have you hunger → Tu as faim
or have you thirst → ou tu as soif
idea_parts: second question → ou tu as soif
exercises.target_answer: Tu as faim ou tu as soif
exercises.meaning: Are you hungry or are you thirsty?
exercises.explanation: Both faim and soif take tu as, linked by ou ('or', no accent).

diagnosis.cue: Use Tu as faim ou tu as soif.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Elle a raison, nous avons besoin de repos
exercises.target_answer: Elle a raison, nous avons besoin de repos
exercises.meaning: She is right, we need rest
exercises.explanation: Elle a raison + nous avons besoin de...
exercises.affirmation: You used both avoir idioms accurately!

summary.outcome: Express hunger, thirst, heat, cold, fear, rightness, and need with avoir + bare noun.

use_example.german: J'ai froid et j'ai faim — allons au bistro !
use_example.english: I'm cold and I'm hungry — let's go to the bistro!

summary.takeaway: People 'have' hunger, thirst, cold, heat, fear, and reason with avoir.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([2902] The Register Ladder Recap): see how Have-Hunger & Co leads directly into The Register Ladder Recap.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "Are you hungry or are you thirsty" in French:
twist.target_answer: Tu as faim ou tu as soif
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Tu as faim ou tu as soif" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Have-Hunger & Co.

faim.context_translation: I am very hungry (lit. I have hunger).
faim.etymology_derivation: French possesses physical states with avoir: avoir faim, avoir soif, avoir froid, avoir chaud, avoir raison.

soif.etymology_derivation: Used with avoir without an article: avoir soif.

peur.context_translation: I am afraid (lit. I have fear).
peur.etymology_derivation: Latin pavor → peur. Feminine abstract noun.

raison.context_translation: You are right (lit. You have reason).
raison.etymology_derivation: To be right in French is to 'have reason'.

besoin.context_translation: I need help (lit. I have need of help).
besoin.etymology_derivation: Triggers dont in relative clauses because of its built-in de.

avoir.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre = have. The H dropped and stayed dropped — French never pronounces its Latin H.

jai.etymology_derivation: je + ai with the vowel sacrificed — elision again, the apostrophe marks the cut.

as.etymology_derivation: Pronounced /a/ — the final s stays silent unless followed by a vowel.

très.etymology_derivation: Latin trāns 'across' — très means 'beyond, across the line'. English kept the same root in transmit and transatlantic.
